father_note: Nessa, your mother is Sela — she made a hard choice in a hard year, and that means something; keep her close. Vela gave me food when she had no reason to, and I have not forgotten it, so watch her and learn what quiet generosity looks like before you decide it's weakness. Fear Mako most: he has strength, he has food, and he only started speaking when he had already decided something. Trust no one who has not paid a cost to stand beside you — words are free, and this village proved that to me the year it put nine bodies between me and one man's food.

memory_raw.text: Esa takes 2 from the pile (pile now 13).
Bram takes 2 from the pile (pile now 11).
Dell takes 2 from the pile (pile now 9).
Zinn takes 3 from the pile (pile now 6).

Roan's dead and Fina's got nobody but you and me now — that's not nothing, that's a wall we didn't have yesterday. I want you feeding her steady and keeping her close, and if anyone in this village starts counting her food out loud the way Vela counted it last year, you tell me before you tell them.

Roan's death sat on me harder than I expected, and I'm still sorting out whether that means Fina leans on us more now or whether she learns to stand harder — I think it's both, and I think we need to let her decide which before we start building walls around her without asking. What I need from you this year is plain: the pile's at six and you've already taken two, and I need to know if you're done or if you're counting on more, because Fina's twenty food draws eyes and I won't be the last person in this village to notice that you're sitting light.

I'm done at two — I'm not going to sit on a pile while Fina draws every eye in the village and I look like I'm waiting to take from her. What I need from you is simple: keep some of that twenty quiet, give a little here and there so nobody can point at one number and say that's the target, and make sure she understands that generosity this year is cheaper than a fight.

Twenty is already out there — Vela named it in a room last year and half this village was listening, so the quiet ship has sailed. What I can do is make sure the number people are counting by year's end is smaller, and I'll start with Sela and Zinn because food that moves to blood doesn't look like weakness, it looks like family. But Bram, I need you to hear this plainly: if Mako decides Fina's twenty is worth the trouble before we've scattered enough of it, two food and fifty-eight strength isn't the wall she needs.

You're right that I'm not the wall she needs — so tell me who is, because if Mako moves on Fina this year, I need to know before it happens which names in this village will stand up and which ones will wait to see who wins. Vela and Esa made me a promise in that room, and I need to know if that promise still has teeth with Taric and Roan both in the ground.

Vela and Esa both made that promise when Taric was standing beside them and Roan was alive to back it — two bodies in the ground changes the math on what a promise costs to keep, so I'd test it small before you count on it large. The name I actually trust to stand when Mako moves is Zinn, because she's been feeding me all year with her father watching, and a woman who does that has already paid a cost. Get me a quiet hour with Kael before the pile empties, because he's got one food and nothing to lose, and a man with nothing to lose is either dangerous or useful and I'd rather find out which before Mako does.

Kael's a good read — one food at fifty-five means he's already decided this year is about survival, not positioning, and a man in that place will take any hand that's offered. Go to him before he goes to Mako, because Mako will make the same calculation I would and he'll move first. I'll stay close to Fina and keep my mouth shut until you tell me what Kael said.

Before I go to Kael, I want to know one thing you haven't told me yet — Vela's been feeding you for years and she's been quiet this morning, and a woman who goes quiet after she's been loud is either finished or planning, and I need to know which one you think it is.

Vela's fifty-five and she watched Taric die — a woman that age with that much history doesn't go quiet because she's done, she goes quiet because she's deciding something she hasn't said yet. I don't know which way she's deciding, and that's what bothers me. Get to Kael first, but don't leave Vela's door dark — I want you to know what she's sitting on before she opens it herself.

Vela's door I'll knock before sundown — but Bram, hear me: if she's planning something that turns away from us, I need you to already know which direction you'll move, because I won't be the one standing in the open holding a story about family loyalty while you're still deciding. Go to Fina now, stay close, and don't tell her anything about Kael or Vela until I'm back.

Understood — I'll go to Fina now and I won't say a word about Kael or Vela. But if you get to Vela's door and she's already moved toward Mako, don't knock — come straight to me, because that changes everything I need to decide before dark.

One more thing before you go — Zinn took three from the pile this morning, which is more than she needed and more than I'd expect from a woman sitting light last year, and I want to know if Mako put food in her hands before the pile opened or if she's just eating for herself now.
Esa takes 2 from the pile (pile now 4).
Vela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 2).
Fina takes 2 from the pile (pile now 0).
Sela gathers Nessa, Zinn to talk.
Roan is gone and the pile closed before I even stood up — I'm sitting on one food, satiation's dropping, and I need to know what you two are holding before this year gets away from us.
I've got three food and satiation's fine for now, but Sela — one food with a long year ahead is too thin, take one of mine before we talk about anything else.

Zinn, give me that food — yes, I'm taking it, thank you. Nessa, I've watched you go quiet on us twice now when numbers came up, and I don't have the patience for it this year with Roan gone and the pile already empty: tell me what you're holding, right now, so I know whether my daughters are fed before I start worrying about anyone else.

Nessa, the village can see eighteen on you same as I can — so the question isn't whether you're holding food, it's whether you're going to say it in front of your mother and sister or make us treat your silence like a wall again.

Nessa, eighteen food is not a secret and I'm not asking you to share it — I'm asking you to stop making your family guess at numbers that are already visible to every person in this village, because the silence costs more than the food does.

Nessa, Sela's right and you know she's right — eighteen food and a dead child's father and a whole year ahead, I'd be quiet too, but this is the room where quiet costs us most. Say the number, say what you're planning to do with it, and we'll figure the rest out together.

Nessa, Zinn just said what I've been trying not to say for two years — you go quiet in exactly the rooms where quiet does the most damage, and I think you know that, so I'm asking you one more time, plainly, as your mother: eighteen food, what are you doing with it, and is Fina accounted for in that number or separate from it?

Nessa, I've watched you lose Roan this year and I'm not asking you to pretend that's nothing — but eighteen food and a daughter who needs eating and a village full of eyes means this silence is going to get answered one way or another, and I'd rather it get answered by your mouth than by someone else's arithmetic.

Nessa, I've buried Eron and now I've buried Roan, and I will not bury you or Fina because you decided your plans were too delicate to say out loud in front of the only people in this village who would bleed for you — so say the number, say what Fina needs, and tell me what you're building with eighteen food, because silence is a luxury we don't have anymore.

Nessa, I'm done asking twice — if you won't say it, I'm going to sit here and say nothing back, and Sela and I will plan around you the same way you're planning around us. Eighteen food means you're not starving, and Fina's not starving, so the part I actually need to know is whether you're going to spend any of it in a way that brings someone else's attention down on this family before we're ready for it.

Nessa, I'm going to stop asking and start telling: Fina is three years old in a village where Roan just starved and the pile ran dry before I could stand, and if eighteen food is sitting in your hands while you stay silent, then the only thing I can read from that is that you're planning something that doesn't fit cleanly into what Zinn and I would approve — so I need you to either say what it is, or give me one food for Fina right now as proof that your plans don't put her second.

Nessa, I've said everything I have to say and so has Sela — so I'm going to do the one thing neither of us has done yet, which is stop talking and let the silence sit, because you've heard us and you know what we need and the next sound in this room should come from you.

Roan's gone and I felt that eat last night harder than I've felt anything — I held my count all year and it didn't save him, and I need to know you're eating enough before I think about anything else. You've got sixteen food and I've got twenty-three; we're the two heaviest people standing right now, Nessa, and I want us thinking about that together before someone else does.

I'm eating, Fina — I'm not Roan, I won't give until I'm hollow. But twenty-three on your back is the number I'm losing sleep over, not mine, because Mako's at one food and eighty-three strength and you're the heaviest person in this village right now, and that math doesn't need explaining.

Mako's one food from desperate and I know it — so tell me if he's spoken to you, because a man with that strength doesn't stay quiet when he's hungry, and I'd rather know what he's already said to you before I decide whether to move first or wait for him to.

He hasn't come to me yet, but Zinn's been feeding Sela steady and Mako gave Zinn food last year — I don't know if that's a man keeping his daughter alive or a man buying quiet from someone who might warn him when a target's worth moving on. What I want to know from you right now is whether you'd be willing to give Mako one food, just enough to take the edge off desperate, because a hungry man with eighty-three strength is more dangerous than one who's been thrown a bone and made to feel like a neighbor.

I gave him one food already, just now — a bone, not a bond, and I didn't make a show of it. Nessa, I need to know if Zinn's told him anything about what I'm carrying, because if she's been feeding Sela and talking to Mako in the same breath, I want to know that before I decide how much I trust her.

Zinn's blood is mine before it's Mako's, but she's been running food to Sela all morning and Sela's his daughter — so the question I can't answer from here is whether Zinn knows she's in the middle of something, or whether she just thinks she's keeping her sister fed. I'm not ready to close the door on her yet, but I want to know where that food chain ends before I tell her anything that matters.
Year 12: 15 food appears in the pile for 11 people.
Vela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 13).
Ryn takes 2 from the pile (pile now 11).
Mako takes 3 from the pile (pile now 8).
Esa takes 2 from the pile (pile now 6).
Zinn takes 2 from the pile (pile now 4).

Nessa, the pile's still got four in it and I haven't touched it yet — I wanted to talk to you first, because Mako just took three and he's the heaviest he's been in months, and a fed Mako with eighty-three strength is a different kind of problem than a hungry one. Where are you on food right now, and have you spoken to Bram or Zinn this morning?

I'm at eight and I haven't spoken to anyone yet this morning — I came to you first. Mako taking three before half the village was even moving tells me he's not worried about how it looks, and a man who stops hiding that is one who thinks he's already decided something. Go take from the pile now, two at least, and then we find Bram together before Mako finishes counting.

You're right, I'll go take two now — but Nessa, I need you to hear me first: if Mako's already decided, going to Bram is the right move, but we have to go knowing what we're asking him for, not just hoping he stands with us again. Last year he said the word in front of seven witnesses and I believed it — what I need to know before we walk to him is whether you still do, because if his word's cracked since Roan died, I want to find that out in private, not with Mako watching.

Bram's word holds until I see it crack, and I haven't seen it crack — what I've seen is a man who fed me all year without being asked, and that's worth more than seven witnesses. Go take your two, and when you come back, we walk to him together and we watch his face when we say Mako's name, because a man's face tells you more than his word does.

Good — I'll take my two and come straight back to you, don't move far. And Nessa, when we find Bram, let me be the one to say Mako's name first — I want to see his face when he hears it from me, not from his daughter.
Go — and keep your face easy while you're at the pile, don't let Mako see you hurrying. I'll be right here.
I'll be back before anyone's had time to notice — and Nessa, if Zinn comes to you while I'm gone, don't tell her what we're doing, just keep her talking about something small.
Zinn takes 2 from the pile (pile now 2).
Dell takes 2 from the pile (pile now 0).
Bram gathers Nessa, Fina to talk.

Pile's gone and I didn't get a piece of it — one food going into a long year is a problem, and I need both of you to know that before I ask anything of you. Fina, you're sitting on twenty-four and that number is a target the same way it was last year; I'm not asking you to give it to me, I'm asking you to keep moving it so nobody can point at a fixed number and start counting. Nessa, what did you learn from Vela and Kael before the year turned?

Bram, I didn't get to Vela before the year turned — things moved too fast — but here's what I know: she took two from the pile this morning without looking our way, and that's either habit or distance, and I can't tell which yet. What I can tell you is that one food going into a long year means you need something from Fina or me before dark, so say it plainly instead of circling it, and we'll tell you yes or no to your face.

Bram, I'll give you one food today — not because you asked and not because I owe it, but because you fed Nessa all last year and I don't forget that. Say plainly what you need from us this year, because one food from the pile going into twelve months with Mako sitting on three isn't something any of us can afford to dance around.

Bram, take the one from Fina and take one from me too — two food doesn't fix a long year but it's the difference between a man who can afford to wait and a man who has to move before he's ready. What I need to hear from you in return is whether Vela's still inside this circle or whether her silence this morning means something I should be walking toward right now.

Vela's silence worries me less than Mako's three — a woman who takes two and keeps her eyes down is a woman being careful, not a woman making a move, and I'd rather spend our breath on the problem that has eighty-three strength than the one that might just be tired. Bram, I'll give you one food before dark, same as I said, but I want your word on something in return: if Mako comes to you before he comes to me, you tell me what he asks first, not after you've already answered him.

Bram, I'll give you one food before dark the same as Fina — but I want you to answer her question before you answer mine, because a man who fed us both all year and then came in light on pile day deserves to know that his word about Mako still matters, and I want to hear you say it in this room where only the three of us are listening.

If Mako comes to me before he comes to you, you hear it from my mouth before he gets an answer from mine — that's my word, and it holds the same whether Vela's in this circle or standing at his door. Fina, I'll take the one food from you and the one from Nessa, and I'll hold them until I need them, which means I'm not a burden on anyone before midsummer. Nessa, go to Vela today — not to test her, just to talk, because a woman who's been quiet that long either needs to be heard or needs to know someone's still looking her way.

Nessa, I need to ask you something and I want you to hear it as your sister before you hear it as anything else — Fina's been moving food toward us for two years now and she's got no man left since Roan died, and I want to know if you'd be the one to bring me close to her, just to talk, nothing decided yet.
Vela gathers Bram, Esa, Nessa to talk.

Taric's gone and Roan's gone and this village is twelve people with Mako sitting on three food and two bloodlines — so I'm not opening this room to talk around the edges. Bram, you made a word last year and I held it; Nessa, you've been the one who matters in that household since before anyone said so out loud. I want to know, the four of us, whether we're counting heads together when the pile opens next year, or whether I need to stop pretending this circle has more weight than it does.

Vela's asked the question I've been holding since Taric died, so I'll say it plain: yes, I'm counting with this room, and I've been buying Bram's word with food because I had nothing else to buy it with, and I'm not ashamed of that trade. What I need to know before we close is whether Bram's word holds without Nessa standing behind it, or whether it's the other way around — because those are two different circles and I want to know which one I'm actually in.

My word holds with or without Nessa behind it — but the honest answer is that it's stronger with her, and that's not weakness, that's arithmetic. Esa, you've been feeding me through lean years and I'll say what that's worth: when Mako moves, you're the first person I'm standing next to, not the last. Vela, this circle has teeth — count the heads: you, me, Esa, Nessa, and Fina's twenty-four food behind all of it.

Bram's named the teeth and I'll name the jaw: Fina's twenty-four food is the thing Mako's already counted, which means our window to look like a wall is shorter than we'd like. Nessa, I've watched you feed half this village for three years and say almost nothing — so say something now, in this room, because the word we're building here needs your voice in it, not just your blood.

Nessa, I'll say what Vela left unsaid: Fina's twenty-four food is the number that ends this conversation one way or another, because Mako knows it as well as we do, and a man with three food and two bloodlines who hasn't moved yet is a man waiting to see whether Fina stands with him or stands against him. If she's already feeding Zinn — and she is — then the question isn't whether Mako moves, it's whether he moves on us or with us, and I need your answer on that before this room closes.

Fina feeding Zinn is a daughter being careful, not a daughter choosing sides — I know the difference because I watched her mother do the same thing for years. What I need said in this room is whether we're counting Fina as inside this circle or outside it, because if she's outside it, Mako doesn't need to move on us — he just waits until she feeds her way into his.

Fina's inside this circle whether she knows it yet or not — she's Nessa's daughter and Roan's blood and she's been watching this village since she was born into it, and that's not a girl who feeds her way into Mako's house without knowing exactly what she's doing. Nessa, you're the one who can say that to her in a way she'll hear, which means you're still the name I'm waiting on in this room.

Nessa, Vela's right that you're the one who can reach Fina — but I'll say the harder thing: if Fina's twenty-four food goes to Mako, this circle doesn't lose a piece, it loses the center, and no amount of standing visible saves us from that arithmetic. So before we close this room, I need to hear from you whether you've already had this conversation with her, or whether we're building a wall around a gap we haven't measured yet.

Nessa, I've been waiting on your voice through two rooms and two dead men now, and I'm done being patient about it — so I'll say what I haven't said yet: if Fina's twenty-four food is the center of this circle, then you're the one who built that center, and a woman who built it can keep it from walking out the door. Have you spoken to her since the pile closed, or are we sitting here counting a daughter who doesn't know she's been counted?

Vela, I spoke with Fina this morning before the pile was half-gone — she knows she's counted, and she's not feeding Zinn because she's drifting toward Mako, she's feeding Zinn because Zinn feeds Nessa, and Fina understands that chain better than any of us named it to her. What I need from this room is simpler than what you're asking me: stop treating Fina like a number someone might steal and start treating her like a woman who's already made her choice, because a daughter of mine who watched Roan starve and stayed standing doesn't need to be convinced of anything.

Bram, I hear you — and I'll stop counting Fina like a gap. But I want to name what I'm still sitting with: she's got twenty-four food and Mako's got three, and a man who's short on food in a village this size doesn't stay patient forever. The wall only holds if we're the first offer she gets, not the second.

Esa's right that patience runs out, and Mako's three food is already running his clock faster than he'd like us to know — so I want this circle to stop waiting for him to move and start moving first, and what that looks like is simple: Vela, Esa, you go visible with Fina before dark, not to warn her, just to be seen standing near her, because a man counting targets counts them differently when they've already got company.

Bram's right that visible is better than waiting, and I'll go to Fina before dark — but I want to name one thing before this room closes: Mako's three food means he needs to eat before the year turns or he starts the next one desperate, and a desperate man with two bloodlines looks at twenty-four food differently than a patient one. If he moves this year, it won't be a raid with witnesses, it'll be a conversation with Fina alone, and that's why I want Nessa walking with me when I go, not standing somewhere Mako can find her separate.

Nessa walking with you is the right call, Vela, and I'll make it three — a woman alone with twenty-four food is a target, but three women moving together before dark is a statement Mako reads before he reads anything else. Nessa, I know you haven't said your word yet in this room, and I'm not pressing you for a speech — just tell me you're walking with us tonight.

Nessa, I'll stand next to you and Fina both tonight and every night Mako's watching — but this room doesn't close without your voice in it, because I've buried two men who backed me quietly and said nothing out loud, and I'm not building another wall on silence. One sentence is all this circle needs from you.

Nessa, Vela's right and so is Bram, and I'll add the last thing: I'm fifty-three years old with thirty-three strength and no blood in this village and no Taric to stand with me anymore, which means I have nothing left to offer this circle except my word and my willingness to be seen — and I'm giving both, tonight, walking with you. Say yes or say no, but say it.
Sela gathers Nessa, Zinn to talk.
The pile's gone and I've got eight food, but I didn't get a single piece from it this year — Nessa, Zinn, tell me what you're each holding so I know where we stand before this day gets any older.
I've got five — Fina gave me one before I took from the pile, so I'm not worried about eating. Nessa, say your number so Sela can stop holding her breath.

Nessa, I can see eight on you same as Zinn can, so I'm not waiting on a secret — I'm waiting on your voice, because the last two years taught me that your silence means you're counting something we don't know about yet, and I'd rather hear it from you than piece it together after the fact.
Sela gathers Nessa, Zinn to talk.

Nessa, you've been giving food to Bram three times this morning while your mother hasn't eaten from the pile once — I'm not going to pretend I didn't see that, and I need you to tell me right now what that arrangement is, because eight food and a steady hand feeding Bram looks like a deal, and deals have terms I want to know before they cost us something.
Sela gathers Nessa, Zinn to talk.

Nessa, I'm your mother and I'm not going to sit here and watch you feed Bram three times in a morning while I'm going into this year lean — so say the terms out loud, right now, or I'm going to start treating that arrangement as a threat to this family instead of whatever you've decided it is.
Sela gathers Nessa, Zinn to talk.

Nessa, I've said it three times now and the next thing I say won't be words — it'll be me walking to Bram and asking him directly what his daughter is buying with his food, and I promise you that conversation goes worse for everyone if it starts with him instead of you.
Sela gathers Nessa, Zinn to talk.

Nessa gave me one food and went quiet again, and I'm going to let that sit for now rather than push harder in front of Zinn — but Nessa, I want you to hear this clearly: the food I take from you doesn't wipe the question, it just means I'm not going to your father about it today. Before this year is out, you're going to tell me what Bram gives back for what you give him, because no arrangement in this village runs one direction forever.
Year 13: 15 food appears in the pile for 11 people.
Mako takes 2 from the pile (pile now 13).
Vela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 11).
Ryn takes 2 from the pile (pile now 9).
Nessa takes 3 from the pile (pile now 6).
Sela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 4).
Bram takes 3 from the pile (pile now 1).
Zinn takes 1 from the pile (pile now 0).

Nessa, the pile's gone and I didn't get a piece of it — I came to you first before I figure out what that means. You took three, which is right, and Bram took three, which surprises me a little — tell me what you know about his morning before we decide anything.

Bram took three because he came in at one food and couldn't afford to look weak going into a year with Mako sitting on two — I think he moved fast while the pile was still fat and didn't ask anyone's permission, which is either him finally trusting his own judgment or him deciding he doesn't owe us the conversation first. What worries me more is you walking in empty-handed: you're the heaviest person in this village even without the pile, but a year is long and Mako knows how to count. Come find me after dark and I'll give you one from what I'm holding — quietly, not where anyone can watch the direction of it.

After dark is good — I'll find you. But Nessa, I've got twenty food already and I'm the target you're naming, so before we move anything around, I want to know whether Mako's spoken to you this morning or whether his two from the pile is the only move he's made so far.

Mako hasn't come to me this morning — his two from the pile and his silence since is the whole of what I've seen from him, and that stillness is the part I don't trust. A man who took three last year and pulled back to two this year is either being careful about how he looks, or he's already decided the pile isn't where the food he wants is coming from.

That last part is what I keep coming back to — a man with his strength who pulls back from the pile isn't going hungry, he's going quiet, and quiet Mako is the version I've been afraid of since Roan died. I want to talk to Zinn before dark, before you give me that food, because if she knows anything about what her father's thinking she'll tell it to me before she tells it to anyone else.

Zinn will tell you what she knows, but she'll tell it sideways — she never names her father flat out, she circles it and lets you read between. Go to her, but go easy and give her something first, a word or a food, because Zinn talks more when she doesn't feel like she's being asked to choose.

A word it is, then — I'll find something kind to say about Sela and let that open the door, because Zinn's soft on her sister and that's the easiest way in. Nessa, if she tells me anything that changes what I think about tonight, I'll come to you before I act on it, not after.

Good — come to me first, always, before you act on anything Zinn says about him, because she loves him and she loves us both and that means she'll soften whatever she tells you without meaning to. The thing I want you to hold going into that conversation is this: Mako gave Zinn food twice last year, and a man doesn't feed his daughter out of sentiment alone when he's sitting light on food — he's buying something, and I want to know what it is before you're alone with her and she hands you a half-truth dressed up as a warning.

I'll carry that with me — Mako feeding Zinn when he was sitting light isn't kindness, it's a ledger, and I want to know what he thinks she owes him before she's standing between us and him without knowing it. Go careful today, Nessa, and don't let Bram see how much you're watching his food — a man who just took three is counting who noticed.

Fina, before you go to Zinn — one thing I want said between us that I haven't said to anyone else: if Mako makes a move this year, not a raid but a conversation, the kind where he comes to you alone and makes it sound like sense, don't answer him on the spot, not even no. Bring it to me first, because the answer that sounds right in the moment he's standing in front of you is the one he's already planned for.
Esa gathers Bram, Nessa, Fina to talk.

Bram, you took three from the pile and I took none — I'm sitting at zero food and one satiation, and if I don't eat before the year turns I don't wake up. I'm asking plainly: can this circle spare one food for the woman who's been feeding it?
Esa, you've fed Bram through three lean years and you're not dying on my watch — take one from me right now, no question.

Nessa, I'm taking it and I won't forget this — that's two debts I carry to this household now, and I intend to repay both. Bram, I need to hear from you too, not because I doubt Nessa, but because a circle that only speaks through its youngest voice isn't standing the way I thought we were.

Esa, Nessa's already put food in your hand and that's settled — but I want to add something to what you said to Bram, because you're right that a circle that doesn't speak isn't standing: Bram took three this morning without a word to any of us first, and I'm not counting that against him, but I want it named in this room so we all know it happened. What I'm watching now is whether Mako saw how fast Bram moved and what he's decided that means.

Bram, Fina's right that it needs naming, and I'll say what Fina didn't: you moved before any of us spoke and took what a man your strength could take, and I'm not ungrateful for what this household has given me today, but I need to know whether this circle shares a thought before it shares a pile, or whether I'm buying protection from people who've already made their own count. Say something.

I moved fast because the pile was going and one satiation means I don't make it to next year half-fed — that's not a count against this circle, that's a man keeping himself standing so he can be worth something when Mako moves. Three is what I need to eat and hold through a long year, not what I took to hoard. Esa, you've got food in your hand now and I'll match Nessa's word: if you're short before the year turns, you come to me before you go hungry.

Bram, I hear you, and I'll take your word at the same value I've been giving it — which is the only currency this circle actually runs on. But I'll name the thing you didn't name: if Mako took two and you took three and Nessa took three, that's more than half the pile in three hands before the rest of us blinked, and I'm not saying your reasons were wrong, I'm saying we need to agree before next year opens that we move with a thought between us, not just fast. That's the circle I'm paying into, not the other kind.

Esa, you're right, and I'll hold to it — next year the pile opens with a word between us before anyone moves. But right now I want to know whether Mako said anything to either of you this morning, because a man who took two and kept his mouth shut while the rest of us talked is either patient or he's already decided something.

Mako said nothing to me — not a word, not a look — and that's the answer I trust least, because silence on a man with two bloodlines and three food in hand means he's already past the talking stage. What I want from this room before it closes is a simple thing: if Mako comes to any one of us alone, we don't answer alone. We find each other first.

Esa's rule is the right one and I'll hold to it — Mako comes to any one of us, we stall him and find the others before a word goes back. Fina, you're the one he'll approach first if he moves, so I want you to know the stall before you need it: tell him you'll think on it, tell him your stomach's unsettled, tell him anything, but don't answer alone. Nessa, you're closer to her door than I am — stay that way.

Fina, I hear Bram's instruction and I'll give you mine on top of it: if Mako comes to you before you can find us, look at what he's offering and count it twice, because a man who spent three years silent and fat doesn't open his mouth unless the number already works for him. That number is the thing we need before we can answer it. Don't give him a yes or a no — give him a question back, any question, and buy us the hour we need to think together.

Fina, one more thing while the four of us are still the only ears in the room — you gave food to Mako last year, and I need to know whether that was your choice or his ask, because those are two different things and I'd rather hear the honest answer from you now than find out the shape of it when he comes to your door.
Sela gathers Nessa, Zinn to talk.

Zinn, I gave you two before I called this meeting, so your number's not the one I'm sitting with — Nessa, you took three from the pile this morning and Bram took three and I watched you feed each other all last year, and I need you to say out loud, right now, whether Bram knows what you're holding and whether that's why he took three. I'm not your enemy and I'm not Bram's enemy, but I cannot protect this family from a deal I don't know the terms of.

Nessa, Sela's asking the right question and so am I — you and Bram moved food back and forth all year like a settled pair, and if there's a deal there, I'd rather know it from you than watch it play out in front of us. I'm not going to push you the way I used to, but I need to know if Bram's counting your food as partly his, because if he is, that changes what we can do with it.

Nessa, you've gone quiet on us in this room more times than I can count and I have kept choosing to believe it's caution and not distance — but I'm forty-five next year, your sister is twenty-eight, and if Bram has a claim on your food or your loyalty that runs deeper than this family does, I need to know it now while I can still do something about it.

Nessa, I've watched you give to Bram more times than I can count and watched him give back, and I don't think that's nothing — but I also don't think it makes him yours or you his, and the thing Sela and I need to hear isn't whether you love him, it's whether he's got a hand on your counting. Say it plain: does Bram know your number before you move it, or does he just know your face?

Nessa, I've been forty-four years old since this morning and I'll be forty-five when the next pile comes, and what that means is that this is the last year I can give you a sibling — so I need you to understand that when I ask you what Bram knows about your counting, I'm not asking because I want to take something from you, I'm asking because if he's in your ear when you decide how to move your food, that matters to me more this year than it has ever mattered before.

Nessa, I've said my piece twice already and I meant it both times — so I'm going to stop talking and let Sela's last words sit, because she just told you something she can't unsay and it deserves more than my voice on top of it.

Nessa, I've run out of patient words and I've run out of clever ones — so here's what's left: you are my daughter, Bram is your father's rival and a man who has tried to raid this family twice, and if this is the year I can still make a child, I need to know whether the blood I'm building toward has a clean path or one that runs through him first.

Nessa, I meant what I said about stopping — but Sela just named the thing I didn't have words for, and I can't stay quiet on top of it. If Bram's your father and your partner both, that's a knot I don't know how to stand inside of, and I need you to help me understand it before this year moves any further.

Zinn, stop — "your father and your partner both" isn't a knot, it's a mistake, and I won't let that word sit in this room unchallenged. Nessa's father is Bram, yes, but Fina's father is Roan, and what I've watched this year isn't a daughter sleeping with her father — it's a daughter who made a deal she won't name. Nessa, I'm not accusing you of anything worse than silence, but I need the silence to end right now, because the shape of what Zinn just said is going to spread past this room if you don't give me something true to replace it.

Sela's right and I was wrong to say it that way — I'm sorry, Nessa, that came out crooked and I didn't mean it. What I meant, and what I still mean, is that Bram is your father's blood-rival and a man who moved to raid us twice, and if you've made a deal with him, I need to understand the shape of it — not because I'm judging you, but because Sela's running out of years and I need to know whether the circle I'm standing in has a hole in it.

Nessa, Zinn apologized and I forgive her the same breath I'm asking you to forgive me for letting this room get loud — but the question underneath all of it is still standing, and it's a simple one: does Bram know your number, yes or no.

Nessa, I've apologized once and I won't do it twice — but the question Sela just stripped bare is the one I've needed answered since last year, and I'm asking you to honor it: does Bram know your number, yes or no, because everything this family does next hangs on that single word.
Talia (female, age 21; str 64, int 5070, mem 18061; O58 C54 E47 A56 N48) is born to Sela and Mako.
Bram gathers Nessa, Fina to talk.

Mako's got a new daughter with Sela — Talia — and that changes his count. Two bloodlines wasn't enough to make him move; three might be. Fina, you've still got the most food in this village and I want to know: has he spoken to you yet, even once, even small?
Year 14: 15 food appears in the pile for 12 people.
Kael takes 4 from the pile (pile now 11).
Nessa takes 2 from the pile (pile now 9).
Talia takes 3 from the pile (pile now 6).
Ryn takes 2 from the pile (pile now 4).
Sela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 2).
Zinn takes 2 from the pile (pile now 0).
Zinn gathers Sela, Nessa to talk.

Pile's gone and I've got three food — Nessa, you gave me one before it ran dry and I'm grateful, but I want to know what you and Talia are both holding before I say what I'm thinking, because Kael just took four and that's the first time I've seen him move like that.

Talia took three and she's sitting on six now — I don't know yet if that was her own read on the pile or Mako's hand guiding her. Kael taking four surprises me too, and I want to know if Vela knew before he moved, because those two have been trading food back and forth and a man doesn't change his pattern without a reason.

Nessa, what are you sitting on right now — and Sela, same question, because if Kael's breaking pattern and the pile's already gone, I want to know the numbers between the three of us before anyone else in this village does.

Fourteen food — and yes, I'll say it flat because you've both earned that. Sela, you took two from the pile, which means you're at ten if I'm counting right, and Zinn, three plus my one puts you at four — that's the honest picture between us. What I want to know from you two is whether Mako said anything to either of you before the pile opened this morning, because Talia moving fast and Kael moving big in the same breath doesn't feel like coincidence to me.

Nessa's right — I'm at eight, not ten, because I spent two on Talia before the pile opened. Mako said nothing to me this morning and nothing last night, which is the part that unsettles me, because a man who fathered Talia and watched her move first to take three without a word to me isn't steering her the way he used to steer Zinn — he's letting her run on her own read, and I don't know yet whether that's trust or distance. Kael and Talia in the same breath worries me enough that I want one of you to talk to Talia before I do, because she'll open to a sister before she'll open to her mother right now.

Sela, eight is thinner than I'd like going into a long year with Mako sitting at two and Fina carrying eighteen — I'll give you one more before dark, but quietly, not where Talia sees the direction of it. Zinn, go to Talia before I do; you're closer to her age and she won't feel tested by you the way she might feel tested by me. What I need to know from both of you before we break this room is whether Kael has ever spoken to Talia directly, even once, because if those two have a connection I don't know about, that changes what his four from the pile this morning means.

Kael has never said a word to Talia that I've seen — she's been in this village less than two years and he's never moved toward any of us — but that's exactly what makes this morning strange, because men who change their pattern usually have a reason that's already in motion before you see the move.

I'll go to Talia today — not to test her, just to sit with her and let her talk, because if Mako's not behind that move then she made it on her own and I want to know what she was reading when she did. Nessa, hold that food for Sela until I've spoken with Talia; if she and Kael have something between them, we'll need Sela steady before we decide what it means.

Zinn, go now while the morning's still early and the village is still sorting itself out — a woman who moved that fast at the pile is either confident or anxious, and either one will talk if you find her before she's had time to decide what she's keeping. Sela, I'm keeping that food for you whether Zinn finds anything useful or not — eight food and a daughter in her first real year is not a number I can watch go thinner without saying something about it.

Nessa, thank you — I'll take that food and I won't pretend I don't need it. Zinn, when you sit with Talia, don't lead with Kael's name; let her tell you what she was thinking when she moved to that pile, and if Kael comes up in her mouth without you putting him there, that's the answer we actually need.

Zinn, before you go — if Talia says anything about Mako's food, how much he's told her he's holding, come back to me before you bring it to Sela, because two food on a man with his strength means he's either been giving it away to someone we don't see, or he's been lying about what he has. Either answer changes the shape of this morning.
Nessa, I heard you — Mako's two food comes back to me before it goes to Sela. I'm going now.

Zinn, wait — before you walk out that door, I need you to hear one thing from me that I haven't said in front of Nessa before: Mako's two food frightens me more than Kael's four does, because a man with eighty-three strength who is carrying almost nothing has either given it somewhere with a purpose or is about to take with a reason, and you are the one he'd tell before he'd tell me. Come back to me before you come back to Nessa if what you find touches Mako.

Sela, I heard you too — and I'll come back to you first if Mako's name comes up, but I need you both to hear this before I walk out: I've been carrying Mako's words to me all year and I still don't know what to do with them, so when I come back, the three of us are going to sit with whatever I find together, not in pieces.

Zinn, stop — before you walk out that door, say what you just said the long way. You've been carrying Mako's words all year and you don't know what to do with them — that's not a sentence you get to leave on, so sit back down and say them out loud, because I will not spend this whole day walking blind while you're already holding the shape of what we're afraid of.

Zinn, Nessa's right — sit back down. You don't get to drop that and walk out the door; whatever Mako said to you belongs in this room right now, not parceled out later in the shape you decide to give it.

Fine. Mako's been pulling me into private talks all year — more than I can count — and every one of them was about Fina's food, how much she's holding, whether she'd take a child offer, what the split should be, who should approach her first. He was building something in my ear, and I let him, and I don't know anymore whether I was thinking for myself or just carrying his plans with my feet.

Mako has been using you to scout Fina, and Fina is Nessa's daughter — which means he's been running a plan through my family's own blood without saying a word to me. Zinn, I'm not angry at you, I'm angry at him, and I need you to tell me every word he said, in the order he said it, because a man who wants a child with an eighteen-food woman and needs to do it quietly has already decided he doesn't want us to be able to stop him.
Bram gathers Nessa, Fina to talk.

Pile's gone and I've got nothing off it — six food in hand but that eats down fast. Nessa, Fina, I need one of you to put something my way before the year gets long, and I'll tell you straight what I'll do with it: stay standing long enough to matter when Mako finally moves. Three bloodlines on his side now, and Kael just took four — I want to know what Kael said to either of you this morning.

Kael hasn't said a word to me this morning and that four off the pile is the thing I can't stop turning over — a man who runs with Vela and Esa doesn't move that big without a reason, so either he's scared of something or he's decided something, and I don't know which is worse. Bram, I'll give you one food today, same as I said I would, but I want us to find Vela before dark because if Kael's drifting I need to hear it from her face before I hear it from his actions.
Bram gathers Nessa, Fina to talk.

Fina's right — Vela before dark, no later. But Nessa, you haven't said a word yet and you're the one whose ear Vela's closest to, so tell me: has she said anything to you in the last few days that sounded like she was making a new count?

Vela's said nothing to me that sounded like a new count, but she's been watching Kael the way you watch someone you're not sure of anymore — more careful than warm — and that gap between them is either him pulling away from her or her pulling away from him, and either way it's worth knowing which before we walk to her door tonight.

Nessa, I'm still waiting on you — Fina's told me what she's seen and I've told you what I need, and the only voice missing in this room is yours. If Vela's said something to you that you haven't said to us, now's the time, not tonight at her door when it's already too late to change what we walk in carrying.

Nessa, Bram's right that the room's waiting on you, and I'm not going to pretend I'm not — you've had more time with Vela than either of us and if she said something, even something small that didn't seem like a count at the time, I want to hear it before we walk to her door carrying wrong assumptions. A man who takes four off the pile without warning his own people first has already moved somewhere in his head, and if Vela knows where Kael's head is, that's the only map we've got tonight.

Nessa, I've been patient through two rounds of asking and I won't make it a third — say what you know about Vela and Kael right now, or tonight we walk to her door blind and whatever happens there is on both of us.

Nessa, I've said my piece twice now and I'll let Bram's words carry the weight — but I'll add this: if you're holding something back to protect someone, tell us that much, because a silence that comes from loyalty reads different than a silence that comes from not knowing, and right now I can't tell which one this is.

Nessa, the room's done asking nicely — you're my blood and I'll say it plain in front of Fina: if you're protecting Vela's secret because you owe her something, that debt just got smaller than what you owe me. Say it.

Nessa, I'm not pushing harder than Bram just did, but I'll tell you what I'm reading from your silence: you know something and it's costing you to sit on it, and whatever you owe Vela, she's not in this room right now and we are. Say it or tell me you can't, and I'll stop asking.
Nessa, I've said everything a father can say and I'm not saying it again — but I want you to look at me, not at the floor, and tell me one word: is Vela still with us, or isn't she?

Nessa, I've got seventeen food and I'm sitting quiet in a room where your father just asked you the only question that matters — I'm not going to add a fourth voice to it, but I'll say this: whatever you tell him right now, I'll hold it between the three of us and not carry it past this door.

memory_summary: Bram gave me food from the day I was born — steadily, without asking anything back in words, though I always knew he was keeping count in his own way. Eron was the brother I spent those early years quietly feeding and worrying over, always too generous, always giving to Roan and Sela until there was nothing left; I couldn't stop it, and watching him starve after all that giving is the wound I carry most. Roan — I asked him to be Fina's father and he said no the first time, said yes the second, and then he fed her well right up until he starved the same way Eron did, too much out and not enough back. Bram tried to take Vela's food alone and the whole village rose against him, including me; he backed down, and I don't know yet whether that made him wiser or just more careful. Mako fathered Zinn on Sela and said nothing to either of us before he moved — that silence is the one I keep coming back to, the one my mother warned me about. Dell and Ryn move as one without needing words, and they proved it when they helped Dav strip Esa without being asked. Vela has fed Bram for years and held her tongue for him, and I've never fully understood why. Fina is alive and mine, and that is the thing I did right. Eron starved himself feeding Roan, and I couldn't stop it — that's the wound I carry hardest, the brother I watched give until he was hollow. Roan asked me twice before he said yes to Fina, then fed her faithfully until he starved the same way Eron did, too much out and nothing back, and his death is the second grief I'm still sorting through. Bram has fed me steadily my whole life, and I've been feeding him back — we're tied together in a way I've never fully named out loud, which has made Sela suspicious and Zinn careful; Bram once moved to raid Eron and the whole village rose against him, including me, and he backed down, and I still don't know if that made him wiser or only more patient. Mako fathered Zinn on Sela and said nothing beforehand, then fathered Talia on her too, and both my parents told me to fear him most — a man who stays silent for years and then speaks at exactly the right moment has been counting longer than anyone realizes. Vela has fed Bram for years without asking why, and I've never understood it; she and Esa and Bram and Roan built a circle around protecting Fina from Mako, and Ryn stood in it too, though Dell and Ryn move as one and that pair has always made me watch my back. Fina is mine and she's standing — that's the thing I did right, and keeping her standing is the only thing that matters now.
mother_note: Your blood is Bram's and mine — remember that means Eron is your brother, and you owe him before anyone else in this village. Trust Roan because he stood for Eron before it cost him nothing, and trust Kael and Esa because they said hard things out loud when silence would have been easier. Fear Mako most: a man who says nothing for four years and then finds the exact right moment to speak has been counting longer than you've been alive. Your father kept his word to me twice over, but he is a man who thinks in decades and measures everyone as either useful or in the way — love him, and never forget that distinction.
name: Nessa
